sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to the Rubin Missingness and MICE Imputation Studio. Observe the scatter plot of one hundred twenty data points. Toggle between MCAR, MAR, and MNAR missingness mechanisms to see which points are censored. Then test Listwise Deletion, Mean Imputation, and MICE Imputation, and watch the real-time sample mean, variance retention percentage, and correlation coefficient update dynamically.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Check this out! When I toggle from MCAR to MAR, points with low X values get their Y values censored! And when I click Mean Imputation, look at that vertical spike of yellow dots—variance retention drops down to 60%, and correlation collapses!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Checkpoint 1. A dataset feature has true population variance sigma squared of 100. Exactly 30% of rows are missing at random and imputed using single mean imputation. What is the resulting sample variance of the imputed feature vector?

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Remember our derivation from Slide 5! Imputing the sample mean adds zero squared deviations for all 30% of missing cells. Apply the formula: sigma squared imputed equals 1 minus p times sigma squared!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Outstanding work! Exactly right. Because each mean-imputed value produces zero deviation from the mean, the numerator sum of squares is scaled strictly by the observed proportion 1 minus 0.30, yielding a deflated sample variance of 70. This crushes test statistics and causes severe Type I errors.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Not quite. Recall the mathematical derivation from Slide 5. Single mean imputation assigns the exact sample mean to all missing cases. Their deviation x-i minus x-bar is zero! Therefore, the sum of squared deviations is multiplied by 1 minus p. With p = 0.30, the new variance is 0.70 times 100, which equals 70.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to the Rubin Multiple Imputation Pooling and FMI Workbench. Adjust the number of imputations M from 3 to 30, and modify the average within-imputation variance and between-imputation variance sliders. Watch how Total Variance T incorporates the finite-sample penalty 1 plus 1 over M times B, and track the Fraction of Missing Information gamma.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the stacked variance bar! As I increase M from 3 to 20, that finite-sample penalty shrinks dramatically! And the Fraction of Missing Information shows us exactly how much of our parameter uncertainty comes from the missing values themselves!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Checkpoint 2. A clinical trial runs M = 5 multiple imputations. The within-imputation variance is U-bar = 4.00, and between-imputation variance is B = 1.50. Calculate the exact Total Variance T using Rubin's formula, and estimate the Fraction of Missing Information. Select the correct option.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Apply Donald Rubin's formulation: Total Variance T equals U-bar plus 1 plus 1 over M times B. Compute 1.20 times 1.50, add 4.00, and then calculate the ratio of the between-imputation component to Total Variance!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Brilliant calculation! With M = 5, the finite-sample correction factor is 1 plus 1 over 5, or 1.20. Multiplying by B = 1.50 gives 1.800. Adding within-variance U-bar = 4.00 yields Total Variance T = 5.800. The Fraction of Missing Information is approximately 1.800 divided by 5.800, which is approximately 31.0%.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Careful! Remember Donald Rubin's finite-sample penalty: Total Variance T equals U-bar plus 1 plus 1 over M times B. With M = 5, 1 plus 1 over 5 is 1.20. Multiplying 1.20 by 1.50 gives 1.80. Adding 4.00 yields 5.800, and dividing 1.80 by 5.80 yields an FMI of approximately 31%.
